questions.question_text:
A physiotherapist records only each patient's grip strength during a check-up.
Is this univariate or bivariate data?

options.text: Univariate — only one variable, grip strength, is recorded for each patient.
Bivariate — because grip strength is measured in two hands.
options.why: The stem records only one grip-strength variable for each patient; it does not say that separate left-hand and right-hand strengths are recorded.

options.text: Bivariate — because many patients are involved.
options.why: Confuses the number of individuals surveyed with the number of variables recorded.

options.text: Cannot be determined without knowing the patients' ages.
options.why: Assumes an unrecorded characteristic affects the classification, which depends only on what is actually recorded.

questions.solution_text:
Only one characteristic, grip strength, is recorded for each patient.
One variable means the data is **univariate**.

questions.question_text:
A car dealership records each car's engine size and its fuel efficiency (km per litre), to see whether the two are related.
Name the two variables in this bivariate dataset.

options.text: Engine size and fuel efficiency.
Car and fuel efficiency.
options.why: Names the individual (the car) instead of the characteristic recorded about it.

options.text: Engine size and the dealership.
options.why: Names the place the data was collected rather than the second measured characteristic.

options.text: Fuel efficiency only.
options.why: Names only one characteristic, but bivariate data must involve two variables.

questions.solution_text:
The two characteristics being recorded are engine size and fuel efficiency.
The variables are **engine size** and **fuel efficiency**.

questions.question_text:
Countries that eat more chocolate per person tend to have more Nobel Prize winners per person.
Does this association prove that eating more chocolate causes more Nobel Prizes to be won?

options.text: No — the association alone does not prove a causal link.
Yes — the strong correlation proves chocolate causes higher intelligence.
options.why: Treats a strong correlation as proof of causation, which it never is on its own.

options.text: No — because the two variables are not bivariate data.
options.why: Misapplies the univariate/bivariate classification to a question about causation instead.

options.text: Yes — chocolate must be the cause because it was recorded first in the data.
options.why: Assumes the order variables are listed or recorded in determines which one is the cause.

questions.solution_text:
The two national measures are associated, but this does not show that one causes the other.
National wealth is a possible third factor: it could affect both chocolate purchases and investment in research.
No — the association alone does not prove a causal link.

questions.question_text:
A study compares adults' shoe sizes with their general-knowledge quiz scores. At every shoe size, scores vary widely, with no consistent pattern linking the two.
Is there an association between shoe size and quiz score?

options.text: No — the study shows no consistent pattern linking shoe size and quiz score.
Yes — because both are numerical variables, they must be related.
options.why: Being numerical does not mean two variables must have an association.

options.text: Cannot say — two variables measured in different units cannot have an association.
options.why: Different units do not prevent two variables from having an association.

options.text: Yes — a large sample size always produces an association.
options.why: Confuses a large sample size with evidence of a relationship between the variables.

questions.solution_text:
An association would show a pattern linking the two variables.
Here scores vary widely at every shoe size, with no consistent pattern.
No association is shown in this study.

questions.question_text:
In coastal towns, the number of surf lifesaving club members and the number of sunscreen bottles sold both increase in summer.
A student claims joining a surf club causes people to buy more sunscreen.
Suggest a possible third factor that could explain both increases.

options.text: Warmer summer weather could bring more people to the beach, increasing both club membership and sunscreen sales.
The claim is correct, since both increase at the same time.
options.why: Treats two variables rising together as proof that one causes the other.

options.text: Sunscreen sales cause more people to join surf clubs.
options.why: It asserts the reverse causal direction without evidence; the association alone proves neither direction.

options.text: The two variables cannot be compared because they are measured in different units.
options.why: Raises an irrelevant objection about units instead of addressing whether the correlation is causal.

questions.solution_text:
Both variables rise in summer, but that association alone does not show that joining a surf club causes sunscreen purchases.
Warmer weather could bring more people to the beach, increasing both club membership and sunscreen sales.
Warmer weather is a possible third factor, rather than a proven explanation from these data alone.

questions.question_text:
A survey records both a person's number of siblings and their age, to see whether the two are linked.
Is this univariate or bivariate data?

options.text: Bivariate — two variables, number of siblings and age, are recorded for the same people.
Univariate — because only the number of siblings is a count.
options.why: Age is also a recorded variable; a variable can be measured rather than counted.

options.text: Univariate — because there is no clear cause and effect between them.
options.why: Confuses the univariate/bivariate classification with whether a causal relationship exists.

options.text: Cannot say without knowing how many people were surveyed.
options.why: Assumes sample size affects the classification, which depends only on how many variables are recorded.

questions.solution_text:
Two characteristics — number of siblings and age — are recorded for the same people.
Two variables recorded on the same individuals means the data is **bivariate**.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains the meaning of the phrase “correlation does not imply causation”?

options.text: The thing you are measuring on the x-axis causes the thing you are measuring on the y-axis
options.why: It incorrectly assumes that the x-variable causes the y-variable.

options.text: If two things are negatively correlated, then if one increases the other decreases
options.why: This describes negative correlation; it does not explain why correlation fails to prove causation.

options.text: Just because two things are correlated, does not necessarily mean one causes the other
If you can easily draw a line of best fit, then there is likely to be strong correlation
options.why: A line of best fit does not establish a causal relationship.

questions.solution_text: Correlation shows that two variables are associated, but it does not establish that changes in one variable cause changes in the other. Therefore, option C is correct.
